title: Limnichopharus khaoyaiensis Seki, Hashizume et Maruyama 2026, sp. nov.
abstract: Limnichopharus khaoyaiensis Seki, Hashizume et Maruyama, sp. nov. (Figs 1–11) Type material. Holotype: THAILAND: NAKHON NAYOK: male ♂, Hin Tung, Hin Tung, Mueang Nakhon Nayok District (alt. 741–759 m), 6.vii.2024, R. Seki & T. Hashizume leg. (KUM) (right hind leg refrigerated in 99% ethanol for DNA analysis). Diagnosis. The new species resembles L. borneensis Miyatake more closely in terms of overall appearance and coloration. However, the completely black head, shorter and narrower reddish maculae on the elytra, ventrites of the thorax at least medially reddish brown, and abdominal ventrites 1–3 coarsely punctured, separate L. khaoyaiensis sp. nov. from L. borneensis which has the head yellow, the reddish maculae on the elytra are longer, reaching almost elytral apices and wider, reaching nearly lateral elytral edges, ventrites of the thorax are black and abdominal ventrite 1 coarsely punctured. And from L. hainanensis Miyatake, L. khaoyaiensis sp. nov. can easily be separated by having smaller body, the elytra covered with sparsely scattered small punctations and lacking rows of coarse punctures near suture, the pronotum mostly black with only lateral sides reddish-brown, and each elytron covered with differently shaped and placed reddish-brown macula. Description (male holotype). TL = 1.35 mm; TW = 1.12 mm; TH = 0.61 mm; TL/TW = 1.20; PL/PW = 0.40; EL/EW = 1.00; HW/PW = 0.68; PW/EW = 0.67. Body small, round-oval, strongly convex, densely covered with suberect, long, rather dense and mostly grey setae. Dorsal surfaces black with reddish-brown lateral sides of the pronotum (except for edges) and longitudinal macula on each elytron. Antennae, mouthparts, legs and ventrites of thorax reddish brown; tarsi yellowish brown except for apical half of terminal tarsomere which is black. Head moderately large, about 0.68 times as wide as pronotum; interocular distance about 0.45 times as wide as head width. Pronotum approximately 2.5 times as wide as long; anterior angles produced, sides narrowed anteriorly, and basal margin produced medially into lobe; size of punctures similar to those on head. Elytra covered with a pair of elongate, weakly oblique reddish-brown maculae extending from basal fourth to near apex, distant from suture and margins; irregularly punctate with dense, moderately coarse and rather shallow punctations. Abdomen (Fig. 4) with 5 ventrites; ventrites 1 and 5 long, subequal in length, each longer than 2–4 combined; ventrites 1–2 and 3–4 laterally coarsely and moderately densely punctured, ventrite 5 finely and rather sparsely punctured; posterior margin of ventrite 5 narrowly and deeply emarginate; postcoxal lines of ventrite 1 complete, somewhat angulate postero-laterally, deep, reaching posterior third of ventrite’s length below coxae, and running parallel lateral margins of ventrite; sternite VIII (Fig. 6) with lateral margins elongate and projecting anteriorly, posterior margin excised medially, surface covered with four pairs of oblique lines antero-laterally; tergite VIII (Fig. 5) widely rounded apically. Male terminalia and genitalia. Male genital segment (Fig. 7) U-shaped, with sternite IX very narrow belt and tergite X rounded apically; apodeme of sternite IX long, expanded at its base. Penis (Fig. 8) elongate, almost straight; penis capsule reduced with weakly developed inner arm; tegmen (Figs 9, 10) with penis guide in lateral view curved as elongated S-shape, apex directed backwards, pointed; penis guide in inner view (Fig. 10) gradually widened from base to near half length, then abruptly tapering towards apex, with apical 1/4 widened with a large triangular notch at apex; parameres (Figs 9, 10) narrow and short, approximately 3/5 as long as penis guide, with single long seta at apex; tegminal strut (Fig. 11) in form of inverted ‘Y’, long. Female genitalia. Not studied. Biology. Only a single specimen of this species was found among the numerous Sticholotidini on the trunk of Cassia fistula L. (Fabaceae). Distribution. Thailand (Khao Yai National Park). Etymology. The scientific name of the species, " khaoyaiensis " is derived from the name of the place where the holotype was collected, Khao Yai National Park, Thailand. Remarks. Unfortunately, the male holotype of L. borneensis, housed at the Ehime University Museum, could not be located (likely missing) and was therefore unavailable for study. However, during the description of the new species, we consulted Miyatake’s (1994) original descriptions and accompanying illustrations of the tribe, genus, and species. Moreover, Wang & Chen (2022) provided photographs of the female holotype of L. hainanensis and its ovipositor, which we used for comparison. Miyatake (1994) unfortunately did not provide illustrations of the genitalia of his described species. Based on the available comparative data, the new species can be confidently distinguished from both previously described species (see Diagnosis of L. khaoyaiensis).

title: Isognathotermes finitimus
abstract: Isognathotermes finitimus (Schmitz, 1916) Figs 5, 13–20, 22, 26–33, 39–41, distribution map: Fig. 38; Table 4 Cubitermes finitimus Schmitz, 1916: 120–124, figs 1–2. Cubitermes speciosus Sjöstedt, 1924b: 256. Syn. nov. Mirotermes (Cubitermes) subarquatus Emerson, 1928: 510–511, pl. XXIX fig. 55. Cubitermes finitimus – Sjöstedt 1926: 221–226. — Snyder 1949: 159. — Bouillon & Vincke 1971: 269. — Krishna et al. 2013: 1920. — Josens & Deligne 2019: 60–61, figs 11, 16. Cubitermes subarquatus – Krishna et al. 2013: 1938. Isognathotermes finitimus – Hellemans et al. 2021: 231–233. Diagnosis As already pointed out by H. Schmitz (1916), a soldier or an imago alone does not allow a confident identification. Indeed, this species is difficult to identify from its morphology since it is in a medium position in the genus Isognathotermes (blue ellipse in the middle of Fig. 22). It is obviously easier to identify this species from its mitogenome: I. finitimus makes a clade well apart from the planifrons clade (Hellemans et al. 2021: 231). If molecular data are not available, the best recognition is reached by a combination of worker’s EVA, soldiers’ mandibles, and geographical origin. The worker has a finitimus EVA and is among the medium-sized workers of the genus Isognathotermes (Fig. 30). The soldier is also medium sized in the genus Isognathotermes (Fig. 28; SHdL = 2.70–3.45 mm), and its EVA can generally be recognized as a finitimus EVA. The forehead has little, or no prominence, and the upper profile is only slightly concave. In comparison with I. planifrons, it has, on average, a higher acceleration of the mandible curvature: ln(SMlpR) - ln(SMldR) = 1.28–2.42 (0.89–2.28 in I. planifrons), that means: mandibles less curved at the base and more so at the tip. In I. planifrons, the soldier has on average slightly more curved mandibles. The imago is also medium sized (Fig. 26) in the genus Isognathotermes (IHdW = 1.47–1.71 mm). This medium-sized species can be confused with several other species with a finitimus EVA: I. planifrons and I. bulbifrons (I. phalloides sp. nov. and I. phallicaecalis sp. nov. have also similar sizes and morphologies but they can be distinguished easily by their caecum). Isognathotermes finitimus can also be characterized by its ecology and chorology: it has always been found in continental forests east of longitude 15°E (but the I. finitimus and I. planifrons areas overlap in the south-west of CAR (Figs 38, 47); other species with a finitimus EVA can be found in this area: I. magniplanifrons sp. nov. with distinctly larger soldiers or I. phallicaecalis sp. nov. and I. phalloides sp. nov. with a characteristic, different caecum. Etymology The epithet finitimus from the Latin finitimus (bordering, close to) doubtless refers to the proximity of C. finitimus with both C. fungifaber and C. zenkeri, discussed at length by Schmitz in the original description. Material examined Sixty samples from 24 locations. Of the 35 old museum samples examined, nine samples were initially labelled as Cubitermes finitimus, four as C. fungifaber, one as C. fungifaber var. elongata, one as C. loubetsiensis, six as C. minitabundus, 11 as C. speciosus, two as C. subarquatus, and one as Cubitermes sp. title: Isognathotermes finitimus
abstract: Isognathotermes finitimus (Schmitz, 1916) Figs 5, 13–20, 22, 26–33, 39–41, distribution map: Fig. 38; Table 4 Cubitermes finitimus Schmitz, 1916: 120–124, figs 1–2. Cubitermes speciosus Sjöstedt, 1924b: 256. Syn. nov. Mirotermes (Cubitermes) subarquatus Emerson, 1928: 510–511, pl. XXIX fig. 55. Cubitermes finitimus – Sjöstedt 1926: 221–226. — Snyder 1949: 159. — Bouillon & Vincke 1971: 269. — Krishna et al. 2013: 1920. — Josens & Deligne 2019: 60–61, figs 11, 16. Cubitermes subarquatus – Krishna et al. 2013: 1938. Isognathotermes finitimus – Hellemans et al. 2021: 231–233. Diagnosis As already pointed out by H. Schmitz (1916), a soldier or an imago alone does not allow a confident identification. Indeed, this species is difficult to identify from its morphology since it is in a medium position in the genus Isognathotermes (blue ellipse in the middle of Fig. 22). It is obviously easier to identify this species from its mitogenome: I. finitimus makes a clade well apart from the planifrons clade (Hellemans et al. 2021: 231). If molecular data are not available, the best recognition is reached by a combination of worker’s EVA, soldiers’ mandibles, and geographical origin. The worker has a finitimus EVA and is among the medium-sized workers of the genus Isognathotermes (Fig. 30). The soldier is also medium sized in the genus Isognathotermes (Fig. 28; SHdL = 2.70–3.45 mm), and its EVA can generally be recognized as a finitimus EVA. The forehead has little, or no prominence, and the upper profile is only slightly concave. In comparison with I. planifrons, it has, on average, a higher acceleration of the mandible curvature: ln(SMlpR) - ln(SMldR) = 1.28–2.42 (0.89–2.28 in I. planifrons), that means: mandibles less curved at the base and more so at the tip. In I. planifrons, the soldier has on average slightly more curved mandibles. The imago is also medium sized (Fig. 26) in the genus Isognathotermes (IHdW = 1.47–1.71 mm). This medium-sized species can be confused with several other species with a finitimus EVA: I. planifrons and I. bulbifrons (I. phalloides sp. nov. and I. phallicaecalis sp. nov. have also similar sizes and morphologies but they can be distinguished easily by their caecum). Isognathotermes finitimus can also be characterized by its ecology and chorology: it has always been found in continental forests east of longitude 15°E (but the I. finitimus and I. planifrons areas overlap in the south-west of CAR (Figs 38, 47); other species with a finitimus EVA can be found in this area: I. magniplanifrons sp. nov. with distinctly larger soldiers or I. phallicaecalis sp. nov. and I. phalloides sp. nov. with a characteristic, different caecum. Etymology The epithet finitimus from the Latin finitimus (bordering, close to) doubtless refers to the proximity of C. finitimus with both C. fungifaber and C. zenkeri, discussed at length by Schmitz in the original description. title: Plesiopachyneura ohtaniensis Saigusa et Emoto 2026, sp. nov.
abstract: Plesiopachyneura ohtaniensis Saigusa et Emoto, sp. nov. (Fig.1A) Type material. HOLOTYPE ♀, labelled: [Aichi, Japan], Ohtani, [35°11′31″N 137°48′25″E, 360 m alt], Upper stream of Sakuma Dam, Tomiyama, April 25, 1976, J. Emoto leg; [HOLOTYPE], Plesiopachyneura ohtaniensis Saigusa & Emoto, 2026. The holotype will eventually be housed in Kyushu University Museum, Fukuoka. Description. Female (Fig. 1A). Size: Body length 7.8 mm; wing length 7.8 mm. Coloration: Head black, densely dark grey pollinose; compound eye blackish-brown, antenna dark brown, greyish brown pollinose. Thorax, including coxae, black to blackish-brown, densely grey pollinose; viewed from above mesoscutum with obscure broad dorsocentral stripes narrowing along sides of prescutellar depression; pleura and coxae more polished than nota. Abdomen polished blackish-brown, posterior part from 7th segment to cerci grey pollinose. Legs yellow; trochanters darker ventrally; femora black at extreme tip; tibiae slightly darkened towards tip; tarsi brown. Wing, including veins and halter, uniformly greyish-yellow; pterostigma very faint, slightly darker than ground colour of wing, narrow, surrounding distal 1/2 of vein R 1, ending distally only beyond tip of R 1. Head (Fig. 1B, C, D) globular, almost as high as long; compound eye large, hemispherical, 7/8 as high as head, slightly shorter than high, with anterior (inner) margin weakly arched at dorsal portion of frons; frons (measured from anterior ocellus to antennal base) 1/2 as long as head height, slightly narrower than 1/5 head width, slightly constricted at middle, bare; face short, 1/2 as long as frons, weakly produced anteriorly, densely clothed with black setae; ocellar tubercle large, black setose, 0.18X as wide as head, close to compound eye, distance between lateral ocellus and eye margin 1/3 of diameter of ocellar tubercle; vertex and occiput densely black setose. Antenna (Fig. 1D) 1.5X as long as head; scape long, more or less compressed, 2X as long as wide, black setose; pedicel 1/2 as long as scape, globular, setose distally; flagellum 3X as long as combined length of scape and pedicel, tapered towards tip, short setulose, consisting of 15 flagellomeres, flagellomeres 14 and 15 almost fused with each other and slender; other flagellomeres as long as wide; flagellomere 13 2/5 as long as flagellomere 1. Palpus (Fig. 1D) 4-segmented, sparsely black setulose; distal palpal segment elongate, at least 3X as long as 3rd palpal segment in dried condition; proboscis short and black. Thorax (Fig. 3A, D). General structure almost as in Pachyneura (Figs 3B, C, E, F, 4A). Lateral lobe of antepronotum black setose, postpronotum bare; proepisternum and prosternum bare. title: Tusothrips kenyensis Masumoto & Okajima, 2026, sp. nov.
abstract: Tusothrips kenyensis sp. nov. (Figs 56, 57, 384–392) Female macroptera. Distended body length about 1.3 mm. Body including legs pale yellow (Fig. 56), but head brown within ocellar triangle and pronotum with a longitudinal brown marking medially; antennal segments I–III yellow, IV brown with basal half yellow, V brown with basal third yellowish brown, V–VIII brown (Fig. 386); fore wings brown at base, apex pale, clavus brown (Fig. 388); prominent body setae brown. Head about 0.6 times as long as width across cheeks (Fig. 384), sculptured with transverse striae at vertex, weakly sculptured within ocellar triangle. Mouth cone very long and reaching posterior margin of prospinasternum (Fig. 385), 1.9 times as long as basal width and 1.6 times as long as median length of ventral surface of head. Postocular setae S2 and S4 minute. Antennal segment II without microtrichia; III weakly rounded at each side, weakly narrowed at distal fourth; IV weakly rounded at each side, narrowed at distal third, pedicellate; V weakly rounded at each side, pedicellate, with a narrow-based inner sense cone; VI rounded at basal half, weakly tapered to apex, weakly pedicellate, with a narrow-based inner sense cone. Ratio length/width of antennal segments III–VIII as follows: 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 3.1, 1.2, 3.0 (Fig. 386). Pronotum about 0.9 times as long as width (Fig. 384), weakly sculptured with a few transverse striae near anterior margin, weakly rugose medially, with about 28 discal setae; PAS1 0.25–0.27 times as long as pronotal median length, about 0.73–0.76 times as long as PAS2; PMS1 developed and about 0.2 times as long as median length of pronotum. Mesonotum sculptured with wide spaced transverse anastomosing striae, with anteromedian CPS. Metascutum with median pair of setae much stouter than mesonotal median setae, 0.42–0.46 times as long as metascutal median length (Fig. 387). Mesosternal endofurca with vestigial spinula (Fig. 385). Hind coxa with a few stout microtrichia on inner dorsal surface (Fig. 389). Fore wing costal vein with 22–23 setae. Abdominal tergite I distinctly reticulate, tergites II–VII sculptured with wide spaced anastomosing striae throughout but weak medially; tergites VI–VIII with S4 reduced to minute; tergite VIII with microtrichia arising from sculpture near posterior margin outside of S2 (Fig. 390); tergite IX about 1.2 times as long as tergite X; tergite X slightly shorter than basal width; major setae on tergites IX and X much stouter than major setae on other tergites; distance of S1 on sternite VII narrower than distance of S1 on sternite VI. Ovipositor about 2.0 times as long as pronotal median length. Measurements (holotype female in microns). Distended body length 1310. Head length (including anterior prolongation) ca 73, ventral length 105, width across compound eye 120, width across cheeks 115; compound eyes dorsal length 45, width 33. Mouth cone length 145, basal width 75. Pronotal median length 133, width 146; PAS1 length 33–35, PAS2 length 45–46, PMS1 length 25–28. Metascutal median length 60; median pair of setae length 25–28. Abdominal tergite IX median length 78; S1 length 94–95; S2 length 85–89, S3 length 77–78, MD length 55–58; tergite X median length 65, basal width 69; S1 length 84–86, S2 length 77. Head length (including anterior prolongation) 61–73, ventral length 90. width across compound eye 113–115, width across cheeks 103–105; compound eyes dorsal length 44–51, width 33–35. Metascutal median length 53–54, median pair of setae length 19–23. Fore wing length 500–540, width at middle 30. Abdominal tergite IX median tubercle length 70–77; S1 length 20–25. title: Tretanorhinus nigroluteus Cope 1861
abstract: Tretanorhinus nigroluteus Cope, 1861 Morphology. Tretanorhinus nigroluteus is characterized by having 17–21 dorsal scale rows along the body, with two prefrontals in the cephalic scalation. The number of ventral scales ranges approximately from 133 to 148, while subcaudals vary from 63 to 80 in males and from 56 to 68 in females, indicating moderate sexual dimorphism. Dorsal coloration displays a distinctive pattern: in most adult individuals, a mid-dorsal line composed of alternating dark spots is present, with each spot occupying nearly the entire surface of a single scale (Dunn 1939; Fig. 9). Distribution. Type locality: Aspinwall, Panama, corrected by Peters and Orejas-Miranda (1970). This species has a wide distribution along the Atlantic coast, extending from southern Mexico to Colombia, and occurs on offshore islands such as the Bay Islands (Honduras) and Great Corn Island (Nicaragua; Dunn 1939; Villa 1969; Barquero and Arguedas 2019). In Panama, its distribution extends from the western region to Costa Arriba de Colón and the former Panama Canal Zone (Dunn 1939; Villa 1969, 1970; Ray and Ruback 2015; González and González 2016). We report Tretanorhinus nigroluteus for the first time from the Teribe and Changuinola rivers (Bocas del Toro Province). Based on Dunn’s (1939) morphological description, we identified the subspecies T. nigroluteus lateralis from Donoso (Colón Province) and T. nigroluteus nigroluteus from Portobelo National Park (Colón Province), thereby extending the known distribution of the species by 29 km northeast of its previously documented range. We corrected the locality of specimen MCZ Herp: R-2717, originally listed in the Museum of Comparative Zoology (MCZ), Harvard University database as “ Chiriquí Province ” (georeference: 8.3772°N, 82.1988°W; error radius: 96949 m), assigned by José Rosado on 8 April 2021 using GEOLocate. The correct coordinates are 9.0718°N, 79.6594°W, corresponding to “ Obispo Station, on railway, ” Panama (Fig. 10, Suppl. material 1). Ecology and ethology. Tretanorhinus nigroluteus is a strictly aquatic species, generally found submerged in slow-moving rivers and streams with muddy substrates, particularly along shallow margins of lakes, lagoons, and brackish estuaries with aquatic vegetation or green algae, which appear to characterize its optimal microhabitat. The species is rarely observed on land or basking (Villa 1970). However, González and González (2016) reported an individual moving along a road through a mangrove area; we rescued a specimen in vegetation adjacent to a stream in the town of Portobelo, Colón Province. Water salinity and pH do not appear to be major limiting factors, and water temperatures at sites where individuals have been found range from 24.5 to 27.5 ° C (mean 26.0 ° C; Villa 1970), although further research is needed. Tretanorhinus nigroluteus is crepuscular and nocturnal. During the day, individuals shelter in mud, roots, or vegetation, exposing only the snout for respiration (Villa 1970; Barquero and Arguedas 2019). When disturbed, they dive and seek refuge in rock crevices (Dunn 1939; Villa 1970). The species occurs at low to moderate elevations, typically below 500 m above sea level, although it has been reported at 1200 m in Matagalpa, Nicaragua, where it inhabits isolated ponds or calm sections of rivers (Villa 1970). The diet of T. nigroluteus consists primarily of aquatic animals such as fish, frogs, and tadpoles (Villa 1970; Heimes 2016; Solórzano 2022). Prey items documented in situ include Poecilia sphenops Valenciennes, 1846, Gambusia nicaraguensis Günther, 1866, gobiid fishes, and tadpoles of Rhinella and Incilius (Villa 1970). In captivity, Villa (1970) documented that the species accepts a wide variety of fish, including Alfaro cultratus (Regan, 1908), Awaous transandeanus (Günther, 1861), Bathygobius soporator (Valenciennes, 1837), Amatitlania nigrofasciata (Günther, 1867) which has also been recorded in the wild, Eleotris pisonis (Gmelin, 1789), Poecilia reticulata Peters, 1859, Priapichthys annectens (Regan, 1907), Rhamdia sp., and Cynodonichthys isthmensis (Garman, 1895), as well as adult amphibians such as Craugastor fleischmanni (Boettger, 1892), Dendropsophus microcephalus (Cope, 1886), D. phlebodes (Stejneger, 1906), Scinax staufferi (Cope, 1865), Leptodactylus fragilis (Brocchi, 1877), L. melanonotus (Hallowell, 1861), Lithobates palmipes (Spix, 1824), L. vibicarius (Cope, 1894), and L. warschewitschii (Schmidt, 1857). A recent record of Melgar-Martínez et al. (2022) further expanded the known diet of the species to include freshwater snails Pachychilus largillierti (Philippi, 1843). While being held in captivity for experimental purposes (Fig. 11 A), the individual T. nigroluteus remained submerged throughout the entire observation period, partially or fully exposing only the head (Fig. 11 B). When fish (Astyanax sp. and juvenile Brycon sp.) were offered overnight (20: 00–08: 00 h on 19–20 June 2025), no feeding was observed. In contrast, tadpoles (Rhinella sp. and Engystomops pustulosus) offered on 25 June (five individuals) were consumed within approximately 15 hours, and an additional six tadpoles were consumed on 26 June. To determine whether feeding also occurred during daylight hours, tadpoles were offered in the morning (08: 00 h on 27 June and 10: 00 h on 28 June, respectively). In both cases, all tadpoles offered (eleven and fifteen individuals) were consumed before 18: 00 h. The snake began shedding on 28 June and successfully completed the process on 3 July. When three tadpoles and one metamorph were offered on 3 July (19: 20 h), no feeding was observed until 14 July, when all tadpoles were consumed. The metamorph remained uneaten until 15 July, when it was found dead. On 16 July, during enclosure cleaning, we observed the carcasses had been consumed, suggesting that T. nigroluteus may exhibit necrophagy under certain conditions. Tretanorhinus nigroluteus is oviparous with documented clutches of six to nine eggs (Köhler 2008; Solórzano 2022). Villa (1970) suggested that potential predators of this species include animals associated with aquatic ecosystems, such as herons and Cochlearius or Tigrisoma species, as well as turtles of the genera Chelydra, Kinosternon, and Pseudemys. However, there is currently no direct evidence supporting this hypothesis. First report of a parasite in Tretanorhinus nigroluteus Due to the clearing technique for the parasite specimen, the cephalic end of the worm revealed the esophagus and visible cephalic papillae (Fig. 12 C), structures characteristic of parasites belonging to the genus Eustrongylides (Nematoda). Additionally, structures corresponding to a female (Fig. 12 D) genital primordia were observed. Thus, the observed parasite corresponds to a third-stage larva. This constitutes the first Panamanian record of the nematode Eustrongylides (Ascaridida: Dioctophymidae) parasitizing a snake host and the first worldwide report of this parasite for Tretanorhinus nigroluteus.

title: Capnea japonica
abstract: Capnea japonica (Carlgren, 1940) [New Japanese name: Yosai Isoginchaku] (Figs 2–7; Table 1) Aureliana japonica Carlgren, 1940: 7, 33, 35, 60, fig. IX9–12; Carlgren 1949: 71 (misspelled). Material examined. UUZM 101 (collection of the Zoology Section of the Museum of Evolution, Uppsala University): two syntypes, collected on 6 June 1914, off the coast of Misaki, Sagami Bay, 210 m depth, collected by Dr. Sixten Bock. CMNH-ZG 06547: one specimen, collected on 19 February 2014, off the coast SW of Jogashima, Misaki, Sagami Bay (from 35°06.086′N – 139°34.232′E and 35°05.862′N–139°34.089′E) at a depth of 238– 309m, collected by R/V Rinkai-Maru using a dredge, during a marine faunal research survey conducted by the Japanese Association for Marine Biology (JAMBIO). Description. External anatomy (Figs 2, 3). In freshly collected, living specimen (CMNH-ZG 06547), column orange in color, gradually paler towards the proximal end (Fig. 2A, B); tentacles pale orange with scattered dark orange spots (Fig. 2A). Expanded body, column height ca. 15 mm; oral disc diameter ca. 8 mm, pedal disc diameter ca. 12 mm; pedal disc adherent (adhered to a pebble when collected), circular in outline. In 2 syntypes (UUZM 101), column height 13 mm (small specimen) and 18 mm (large specimen); oral disc diameter 7 mm and 10 mm; pedal disc diameter 11 mm and 15 mm, respectively. In all specimens: scapus smooth, shallow fosse at the distal end (Figs 2B, 3C). Mouth oval, with indistinct lip (Figs 2B, 3C). Tentacles very short, knob like, smaller towards the center from margin (Figs 2B, 3B, C). Outer tentacles largest. Tentacles at least 42 in number (impossible to count all the tentacles in CMNHZG 06547 because of the condition of the specimen), 72 in smaller specimen of UUZM 101 (Fig. 3C), and nocountable in larger specimen of UUZM 101. Two tentacles in each exocoel and endocoel. The siphonoglyph less distinct from external and also internal view (Figs 2B, 3C). Mesenteries (Figs 3D, 4A, B). 20 perfect mesenteries in CMNH 06546 and 18 in larger specimen of UUZM 101. Mesenteries not equally developed within the same pair (Fig. 4A, see the pair numbered 19). Mesenteries at the base more numerous than at the margin. At least 7 pairs of imperfect small mesenteries in CMNH 06545 (Fig. 4A, B). Fertile mesentery not detected in examined specimens. Musculature (Figs 4, 5). Retractors strong circumscript, distinctly restricted (Fig. 4A). Parietobasilar muscles distinct in perfect mesenteries without pennon (Fig. 4A). Columnar circular muscle well-developed (Fig. 4C). Sphincter muscle endodermal, strong pinnate circumscript, elongated, with thick mesogleal main lamella, which strongly fluoresced (Fig. 5A, B). Cnidae (Figs 6, 7; Table 1). Spirocysts, basitrichs, microbasic p -mastigophores. See Table 1 and Fig. 7 for size and distribution. Distribution. Known to occur in Misaki, Sagami Bay, Japan. Bathymetric range 210– 309 m. Phylogenetic analyses. We performed phylogenetic analyses using the concatenated sequences of five regions, resulting in a total of 4159 bp. The resulting trees of the concatenated 12S, 16S, 18S, 28S and COX III DNA are shown in Fig. 8A (maximum likelihood: ML) and Fig. 8B (Bayesian inference: Bayes). Both trees showed Capnea japonica and C. georgiana in the same clade as the suborder Enthemonae (ML=100%, Bayes=1), and it is likely that Capnea is included in the superfamily Actinostoloidea (ML=54%, Bayes=0.994; Fig. 8A, B). Remarks. The newly collected specimen (CMNH-ZG 06547) from the type locality of Capnea japonica possesses very characteristic knob like tentacles, a smooth column, and strong endodermal sphincters. It also has two tentacles within the exocoels and endocoels. These features could support the identification of CMNH-ZG 06547 as a species of Capnea. The only species known from the Pacific is C. japonica. Except for the syntypes, no additional specimens of C. japonica have been recorded. The morphological characters of the syntypes and those included in Carlgren’s original description (Carlgren 1940: 35, 60) were almost the same as those observed in CMNH-ZG 06547. Based on the morphological comparison between the syntypes and CMNHZG 06547, we identified the latter as C. japonica. This is the third known specimen of C. japonica after the two syntypes, collected in 1914. Carlgren (1940) described 18 pairs of perfect mesenteries in the syntypes; however, we found that the smaller specimen had not been dissected. CMNH-ZG 06547 has at least 20 pairs of perfect mesenteries, although it is not a normal arrangement in that the mesenteries within the same pair are unequally developed (Fig. 4A). In the larger specimen of the syntypes, it is difficult to identify the pairs of mesenteries because no histological sections were prepared for detailed observation, and, therefore, we could not examine them. Dunn (1983: 39) said “Up to four cycles of thin mesenteries; regularly arrayed but those of highest cycle may develop asynchronously…”, in the description of C. georgiana. This does not mean asynchronous development of the mesenteries within the same pairs; however, this is not the “regular arrangement.” The mesenterial arrangement of the other Capnea species has not been investigated in detail and therefore further investigation of the developing of mesenteries of Capnea species is needed. Phylogeny of Capneidae. Rodríguez et al. (2014) considered Capneidae to be included in Actinioidea. This might be because Capnea has no characters in common with the other two superfamilies; it has neither mesenteries arranged according to the Actinostola rule, the characteristic feature of the part of Actinostoloidea; nor acontia, a characteristic feature of Metridioidea. Their phylogenetic analyses, however, indicated different results: C. georgiana was nested in the clade of Actinostoloidea, despite the reliability being low. By including C. japonica, our phylogenetic analyses reinforced the hypothesis of Capneidae belonging within Actinostoloidea. In the present study, the mesenterial arrangement of C. japonica. japonica was not the regular arrangement seen in most Actiniidae species. The unequally developed mesenteries within the pair might be because of the ‘ Actinostola rule’ which Carlgren (1949: 77) stated as “In the younger cycles the mesenteries of each pair are usually unequally developed in such a way that the mesentery with turns its longitudinal muscle towards nearest mesentery of the preceding cycle is larger than its partner.” The possession of a strong endodermal sphincter, however, still needs to be evaluated in terms of its origin and homology between the different types of endomyarian sphincters. Also, the development of mesenteries of Capnea species should be examined in detail to discuss the phylogenetic relationships between Capneidae and the other family, Actinostolidae, in Actinostoloidea.

Carlgren (1940) described 18 pairs of perfect mesenteries in the syntypes; however, we found that the smaller specimen had not been dissected. CMNH-ZG 06547 has at least 20 pairs of perfect mesenteries, although it is not a normal arrangement in that the mesenteries within the same pair are unequally developed (Fig. 4A). In the larger specimen of the syntypes, it is difficult to identify the pairs of mesenteries because no histological sections were prepared for detailed observation, and, therefore, we could not examine them. Dunn (1983: 39) said “Up to four cycles of thin mesenteries; regularly arrayed but those of highest cycle may develop asynchronously…”, in the description of C. georgiana. This does not mean asynchronous development of the mesenteries within the same pairs; however, this is not the “regular arrangement.” The mesenterial arrangement of the other Capnea species has not been investigated in detail and therefore further investigation of the developing of mesenteries of Capnea species is needed. Phylogeny of Capneidae. Rodríguez et al. (2014) considered Capneidae to be included in Actinioidea. This might be because Capnea has no characters in common with the other two superfamilies; it has neither mesenteries arranged according to the Actinostola rule, the characteristic feature of the part of Actinostoloidea; nor acontia, a characteristic feature of Metridioidea. Their phylogenetic analyses, however, indicated different results: C. georgiana was nested in the clade of Actinostoloidea, despite the reliability being low. By including C. japonica, our phylogenetic analyses reinforced the hypothesis of Capneidae belonging within Actinostoloidea. In the present study, the mesenterial arrangement of C. japonica. japonica was not the regular arrangement seen in most Actiniidae species. The unequally developed mesenteries within the pair might be because of the ‘ Actinostola rule’ which Carlgren (1949: 77) stated as “In the younger cycles the mesenteries of each pair are usually unequally developed in such a way that the mesentery with turns its longitudinal muscle towards nearest mesentery of the preceding cycle is larger than its partner.” The possession of a strong endodermal sphincter, however, still needs to be evaluated in terms of its origin and homology between the different types of endomyarian sphincters. Also, the development of mesenteries of Capnea species should be examined in detail to discuss the phylogenetic relationships between Capneidae and the other family, Actinostolidae, in Actinostoloidea.

title: Tretanorhinus nigroluteus Cope 1861
abstract: Tretanorhinus nigroluteus Cope, 1861 Morphology. Tretanorhinus nigroluteus is characterized by having 17–21 dorsal scale rows along the body, with two prefrontals in the cephalic scalation. The number of ventral scales ranges approximately from 133 to 148, while subcaudals vary from 63 to 80 in males and from 56 to 68 in females, indicating moderate sexual dimorphism. Dorsal coloration displays a distinctive pattern: in most adult individuals, a mid-dorsal line composed of alternating dark spots is present, with each spot occupying nearly the entire surface of a single scale (Dunn 1939; Fig. 9). Distribution. Type locality: Aspinwall, Panama, corrected by Peters and Orejas-Miranda (1970). This species has a wide distribution along the Atlantic coast, extending from southern Mexico to Colombia, and occurs on offshore islands such as the Bay Islands (Honduras) and Great Corn Island (Nicaragua; Dunn 1939; Villa 1969; Barquero and Arguedas 2019). In Panama, its distribution extends from the western region to Costa Arriba de Colón and the former Panama Canal Zone (Dunn 1939; Villa 1969, 1970; Ray and Ruback 2015; González and González 2016). We report Tretanorhinus nigroluteus for the first time from the Teribe and Changuinola rivers (Bocas del Toro Province). Based on Dunn’s (1939) morphological description, we identified the subspecies T. nigroluteus lateralis from Donoso (Colón Province) and T. nigroluteus nigroluteus from Portobelo National Park (Colón Province), thereby extending the known distribution of the species by 29 km northeast of its previously documented range. We corrected the locality of specimen MCZ Herp: R-2717, originally listed in the Museum of Comparative Zoology (MCZ), Harvard University database as “ Chiriquí Province ” (georeference: 8.3772°N, 82.1988°W; error radius: 96949 m), assigned by José Rosado on 8 April 2021 using GEOLocate. The correct coordinates are 9.0718°N, 79.6594°W, corresponding to “ Obispo Station, on railway, ” Panama (Fig. 10, Suppl. material 1). Ecology and ethology. Tretanorhinus nigroluteus is a strictly aquatic species, generally found submerged in slow-moving rivers and streams with muddy substrates, particularly along shallow margins of lakes, lagoons, and brackish estuaries with aquatic vegetation or green algae, which appear to characterize its optimal microhabitat. The species is rarely observed on land or basking (Villa 1970). However, González and González (2016) reported an individual moving along a road through a mangrove area; we rescued a specimen in vegetation adjacent to a stream in the town of Portobelo, Colón Province. Water salinity and pH do not appear to be major limiting factors, and water temperatures at sites where individuals have been found range from 24.5 to 27.5 ° C (mean 26.0 ° C; Villa 1970), although further research is needed. Tretanorhinus nigroluteus is crepuscular and nocturnal. During the day, individuals shelter in mud, roots, or vegetation, exposing only the snout for respiration (Villa 1970; Barquero and Arguedas 2019). When disturbed, they dive and seek refuge in rock crevices (Dunn 1939; Villa 1970). The species occurs at low to moderate elevations, typically below 500 m above sea level, although it has been reported at 1200 m in Matagalpa, Nicaragua, where it inhabits isolated ponds or calm sections of rivers (Villa 1970). The diet of T. nigroluteus consists primarily of aquatic animals such as fish, frogs, and tadpoles (Villa 1970; Heimes 2016; Solórzano 2022). Prey items documented in situ include Poecilia sphenops Valenciennes, 1846, Gambusia nicaraguensis Günther, 1866, gobiid fishes, and tadpoles of Rhinella and Incilius (Villa 1970). In captivity, Villa (1970) documented that the species accepts a wide variety of fish, including Alfaro cultratus (Regan, 1908), Awaous transandeanus (Günther, 1861), Bathygobius soporator (Valenciennes, 1837), Amatitlania nigrofasciata (Günther, 1867) which has also been recorded in the wild, Eleotris pisonis (Gmelin, 1789), Poecilia reticulata Peters, 1859, Priapichthys annectens (Regan, 1907), Rhamdia sp., and Cynodonichthys isthmensis (Garman, 1895), as well as adult amphibians such as Craugastor fleischmanni (Boettger, 1892), Dendropsophus microcephalus (Cope, 1886), D. phlebodes (Stejneger, 1906), Scinax staufferi (Cope, 1865), Leptodactylus fragilis (Brocchi, 1877), L. melanonotus (Hallowell, 1861), Lithobates palmipes (Spix, 1824), L. vibicarius (Cope, 1894), and L. warschewitschii (Schmidt, 1857). A recent record of Melgar-Martínez et al. (2022) further expanded the known diet of the species to include freshwater snails Pachychilus largillierti (Philippi, 1843). While being held in captivity for experimental purposes (Fig. 11 A), the individual T. nigroluteus remained submerged throughout the entire observation period, partially or fully exposing only the head (Fig. 11 B). When fish (Astyanax sp. and juvenile Brycon sp.) were offered overnight (20: 00–08: 00 h on 19–20 June 2025), no feeding was observed. In contrast, tadpoles (Rhinella sp. and Engystomops pustulosus) offered on 25 June (five individuals) were consumed within approximately 15 hours, and an additional six tadpoles were consumed on 26 June. To determine whether feeding also occurred during daylight hours, tadpoles were offered in the morning (08: 00 h on 27 June and 10: 00 h on 28 June, respectively). In both cases, all tadpoles offered (eleven and fifteen individuals) were consumed before 18: 00 h. The snake began shedding on 28 June and successfully completed the process on 3 July. When three tadpoles and one metamorph were offered on 3 July (19: 20 h), no feeding was observed until 14 July, when all tadpoles were consumed. The metamorph remained uneaten until 15 July, when it was found dead. On 16 July, during enclosure cleaning, we observed the carcasses had been consumed, suggesting that T. nigroluteus may exhibit necrophagy under certain conditions. Tretanorhinus nigroluteus is oviparous with documented clutches of six to nine eggs (Köhler 2008; Solórzano 2022). Villa (1970) suggested that potential predators of this species include animals associated with aquatic ecosystems, such as herons and Cochlearius or Tigrisoma species, as well as turtles of the genera Chelydra, Kinosternon, and Pseudemys. However, there is currently no direct evidence supporting this hypothesis. First report of a parasite in Tretanorhinus nigroluteus Due to the clearing technique for the parasite specimen, the cephalic end of the worm revealed the esophagus and visible cephalic papillae (Fig. 12 C), structures characteristic of parasites belonging to the genus Eustrongylides (Nematoda). Additionally, structures corresponding to a female (Fig. 12 D) genital primordia were observed. Thus, the observed parasite corresponds to a third-stage larva. This constitutes the first Panamanian record of the nematode Eustrongylides (Ascaridida: Dioctophymidae) parasitizing a snake host and the first worldwide report of this parasite for Tretanorhinus nigroluteus.

title: It is time to look back on postmodernism
abstract: The research field of architectural history that I specialize in requires extremely careful judgments in dealing with contemporary cultural phenomena. This is because maintaining a certain temporal distance from the research subject is necessary to determine its historical value or make an objective judgment based on fairness and impartiality. The question of how long this temporal distance should be is difficult to answer and has led to an endless debate. Nevertheless, the number of years required for a historic building to be recognized as a cultural property could be a reference when deciding the adequacy of temporal distance. In Japan, the construction of more than 50 years old is a prerequisite to be eligible as a “tangible cultural property.”1 In fact, after half a century, the architectures considerably lose their lively economic aspects as direct results of construction activities, and can therefore be evaluated neutrally with no conflict of interests. It becomes possible to research about the history of a building if it was built more than half a century ago, and consider it within the social background of that time to evaluate it from a neutral perspective in terms of various aspects. The above-mentioned half-century period required for a building to be upgraded to a “tangible cultural property” is a common feature provided that certain conditions of architectural history research are met. In fact, since the 2000s, research on the postwar era, which is the period dating back to half a century ago, has increased considerably. This includes the reconstruction from war damage, early architectural works, and projects by Kenzo Tange, the Metabolism group, and the period of high economic growth. Now, in 2020, the architecture of the 1970s can finally become the subject of historical research. If the miraculous economic growth of the 1960s showed architectures that reflected the outstanding progress of buildings unique to Japan, in the1970s, Japanese architecture entered a different phase, keeping pace with the world’s architectural scene. Postmodernism can be the key for the historical assessment of this period. The architects who have actively taken part in postmodernism are not keen on looking back to that period and notoriety of such a period cannot be disregarded. Nevertheless, postmodernism will eventually gain sufficient temporal distance to be considered history. This will allow us to evaluate the period with a neutral perspective. Postmodernism in architecture is perceived in various aspects. The postmodern architecture is commonly recognized as a new phase that followed modernism aiming at reflecting on and amending modernist manner, considering the increased awareness of the drawbacks of the modern architectural movement. However, there is a wide range of views on how to differentiate postmodernism from modernism. Whether the criteria are related to the perceptions and way of thinking of each architect involved in the movement or in the style of their architectural works must be determined. Based on the theoretical basis of Robert Venturi’s book, Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966), awareness about postmodernism issues were already developing in the 1960s. However, the architectural movement was not defined until the publication of Charles Jencks’s book, The Language of Post-Modern Architecture (1977). Nevertheless, it is undeniable that in the rise of postmodernism, whether in the 1960s or 1970s, stimulating texts by American architects influenced the world’s architectural scene. At about the same time, a few Japanese architects considered the theories of Venturi and Jencks despite the boundaries of language. Soon after, postmodernism pervaded the architectural world in Japan. Whether from the theoretical or practical aspects of postmodernism as a cultural phenomenon, there is scope for various levels of research from the global to the local perspectives and vice versa. This could be done by inquiring about how postmodernism spread from the United States to the world or determining the differences in the postmodernist cultural acceptance among countries and regions. For example, the postmodernism that was recognized in Japan must be carefully thought over, by considering not only geographical but also temporal dimensions, i.e., how it varies from that of the United States, Europe, or other nonwestern countries as well as the time lag among the various countries. If specific verifications are left as future research topics, it must be noted that Japanese architects gained consciousness of the era of postmodernism not in the 1960s or 1970s but the 1980s, i.e., in the wake of the bubble economy. In the search of a positive meaning in diversity and confrontation, and enjoying the gap between architectural form and its meaning, the explanations that supported the architectural design were shrouded in an extremely intellectual (sometimes even unintelligible, almost esoteric) atmosphere.2, 3 However, these outcomes of favorable times will be seen as objects of reflection during the subsequent recession. In particular, a series of harsh criticisms against the fact that architectural design had become an experiment of intellectual thoughts, divorced from the real world, has been decisive in fixing the majority of the current negative images and evaluations of postmodernism in architecture. References to historical elements in architectural design have been known to be an essential part of the intellectual experimentation of postmodernism. In that respect, postmodernism is also a movement that built up a positive relationship with architectural traditions, which, on the contrary, had been rejected by modernism. Consequently, the degree of understanding of architectural traditions too should be thoroughly considered when assessing the quality of postmodernism at a global or local level. For example, in postmodernism, traditional architectural motifs and decorations were incorporated into the exterior design of new buildings; however, relatively different resulting effects should be expected between buildings built in Western cultural regions, with a completely assimilated rock-solid classical tradition, and those in nonwestern cultural regions where classical architecture was introduced as a foreign design within the national modernization process. Indeed, a difference exists between seizing Greek, Roman, or Renaissance architectures in the Western world and the understanding of such historical monuments in Japan. Moreover, regarding the significance of re-interpreting architectural expressions of such traditions, the intended effects will differ depending on the cultural context of each country. Some theorists determined the sense of postmodernism in terms of historical forms was used in accordance with meanings distant from their original forms. Even if they made such a claim, undeniably, the knowledge of historical architecture was still crucial in the new architectural design. In fact, despite the differences in their elaboration, architectural traditions and historical research did contribute to the development of postmodernist architecture. At this point, the understanding of tradition and the design of contemporary architecture, that is, the knowledge needed for both architectural history research and pursuing new design, coincided. Recalling the development of architectural history research in Japan, the design of Western architecture was understood as part of the revivalism from the Meiji era; however, before World War II, the level of architectural history was not particularly high. After the war, the academic accuracy of Western architecture, as a discipline, increased rapidly. In addition, the level of understanding of Western traditional architecture greatly developed, from the stage of recognizing the masterpieces of a handful of architects, such as Michelangelo and Palladio, as much as possible to the stage where the whole picture of the times, continuity, and changes between the periods were surely grasped. In such academic context, and in particular, within the realm of Western architectural history, it is interesting to note that the late Renaissance period was highlighted as “Mannerism” at the exact time when architectural history started to be used to give meanings to postmodernist design theory and morphological manipulation. The reassessment of Mannerism in architectural history was often discussed by making a parallel between Mannerism and Renaissance as well as postmodernism and modernism. The AT&T Tower by Philip Johnson and the Tsukuba Center Building by Arata Isozaki are taken as easy-to-understand examples, specifically inspired by the latest knowledge of Western architectural history.4, 5 Especially, from the 1970s to the 1980s was a time when knowledge of Western architectural history stimulated architectural design. For architectural history research, which has been rarely directly related to the architectural practice of the present generation, postmodernism was considered as an opportunity to be involved in architectural design for the first time since the Meiji era. Nevertheless, because of its academic nature, architectural history did not provide an immediate historical appreciation to postmodernism because of its contemporaneousness. Now, after more than 50 years, architectural history should regard postmodernism as a subject for academic research and thoroughly examine it as an architectural phenomenon that swept across the 1970s and 1980s. The arguments from different researchers are likely to vary for the following aspects. What part of modernism was postmodernism trying to criticize and revise? Why did postmodernist design practices have to be limited to the morphological level in terms of tradition? Why was the visual image that was created by arranging traditional architectural elements consumed so rapidly and forgotten? However, the topic of issue here, goes beyond the questions of form and design. We can expect new evaluation aspects in terms of structure, equipment, building materials, colors, settings, and relationship with the clients. Currently, on the one hand, the term “bubble heritage” (which refers to the high-quality and luxurious buildings built during the bubble economy, from 1986 to 1991) has also gained research interest.6 On the other hand, works that once attracted great attention in architectural journals have already been demolished. However, now that the works of postmodernism will begin to be considered as possible candidates for the designation of future cultural properties, it is time for casting away any prejudices against postmodernism. By scientifically tackling postmodernism-related themes and finding their proper historical value, the advancement of architectural knowledge could begin.

title: Tusothrips kenyensis Masumoto & Okajima, 2026, sp. nov.
abstract: Tusothrips kenyensis sp. nov. (Figs 56, 57, 384–392) Female macroptera. Distended body length about 1.3 mm. Body including legs pale yellow (Fig. 56), but head brown within ocellar triangle and pronotum with a longitudinal brown marking medially; antennal segments I–III yellow, IV brown with basal half yellow, V brown with basal third yellowish brown, V–VIII brown (Fig. 386); fore wings brown at base, apex pale, clavus brown (Fig. 388); prominent body setae brown. Head about 0.6 times as long as width across cheeks (Fig. 384), sculptured with transverse striae at vertex, weakly sculptured within ocellar triangle. Mouth cone very long and reaching posterior margin of prospinasternum (Fig. 385), 1.9 times as long as basal width and 1.6 times as long as median length of ventral surface of head. Postocular setae S2 and S4 minute. Antennal segment II without microtrichia; III weakly rounded at each side, weakly narrowed at distal fourth; IV weakly rounded at each side, narrowed at distal third, pedicellate; V weakly rounded at each side, pedicellate, with a narrow-based inner sense cone; VI rounded at basal half, weakly tapered to apex, weakly pedicellate, with a narrow-based inner sense cone. Ratio length/width of antennal segments III–VIII as follows: 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 3.1, 1.2, 3.0 (Fig. 386). Pronotum about 0.9 times as long as width (Fig. 384), weakly sculptured with a few transverse striae near anterior margin, weakly rugose medially, with about 28 discal setae; PAS1 0.25–0.27 times as long as pronotal median length, about 0.73–0.76 times as long as PAS2; PMS1 developed and about 0.2 times as long as median length of pronotum. Mesonotum sculptured with wide spaced transverse anastomosing striae, with anteromedian CPS. Metascutum with median pair of setae much stouter than mesonotal median setae, 0.42–0.46 times as long as metascutal median length (Fig. 387). Mesosternal endofurca with vestigial spinula (Fig. 385). Hind coxa with a few stout microtrichia on inner dorsal surface (Fig. 389). Fore wing costal vein with 22–23 setae. Abdominal tergite I distinctly reticulate, tergites II–VII sculptured with wide spaced anastomosing striae throughout but weak medially; tergites VI–VIII with S4 reduced to minute; tergite VIII with microtrichia arising from sculpture near posterior margin outside of S2 (Fig. 390); tergite IX about 1.2 times as long as tergite X; tergite X slightly shorter than basal width; major setae on tergites IX and X much stouter than major setae on other tergites; distance of S1 on sternite VII narrower than distance of S1 on sternite VI. Ovipositor about 2.0 times as long as pronotal median length. Measurements (holotype female in microns). Distended body length 1310. Head length (including anterior prolongation) ca 73, ventral length 105, width across compound eye 120, width across cheeks 115; compound eyes dorsal length 45, width 33. Mouth cone length 145, basal width 75. Pronotal median length 133, width 146; PAS1 length 33–35, PAS2 length 45–46, PMS1 length 25–28. Metascutal median length 60; median pair of setae length 25–28. Fore wing length 590, width at middle 35. Abdominal tergite IX median length 78; S1 length 94–95; S2 length 85–89, S3 length 77–78, MD length 55–58; tergite X median length 65, basal width 69; S1 length 84–86, S2 length 77. Ovipositor length 270. Antennae length 245, segments III–VIII length (width) as follows: 43 (19), 43 (18), 38 (15), 43 (14), 8 (6), 15 (5). Male macroptera. Body color similar to female (Fig. 57). Abdominal tergite IX with S1 arising from a single long tubercle (Fig. 391), S1 0.3 times as long as the tubercle, with a median trapezoidal tubercle beneath median tubercle, with a median forked large tubercle (drepanae) at posterior margin, each arm serrate at inner margin of apex, MD situated outside of median CPS and almost as long as median tubercle, S3 slender, about 0.5 times as long as S2; sternites III – VII each with a transverse pore plate (Fig. 392). Measurements (paratype male in microns). Distended body length 970–1070. Head length (including anterior prolongation) 61–73, ventral length 90. width across compound eye 113–115, width across cheeks 103–105; compound eyes dorsal length 44–51, width 33–35. Mouth cone length 110, basal width 53. Pronotal median length 108–113, width 125–128; PAS1 length 26–35, PAS2 length 38–43, PMS1 length 19–23. Metascutal median length 53–54, median pair of setae length 19–23. Fore wing length 500–540, width at middle 30. Abdominal tergite IX median tubercle length 70–77; S1 length 20–25. Pore plates length (width) on abdominal sternites III–VII as follows: 8–11 (53–65), 8–10 (58–65), 8–10 (55–66), 8–10 (58–65), 8–10 (53–60). Antennae length 224, segments III–VIII length (width) as follows: 38 (15), 35-38 (15-16), 35 (14–15), 40–41 (14), 8–9 (5), 14–15 (4). Type series. Holotype: female, Kenya, Nyahururu, on leaves of Njuriga (=? Coffea species [Rubiaceae]), 6.ii.1999, JM. Paratype s: Kenya, 34 females & 10 males collected together with holotype; Nairobi, Nairobi Museum, 7 females & 3 males on Abyssinica dry leaves (=? Blubine abyssinica or Euphorbia abyssinica), 6. vii. 1999, JM. Holotype and most paratypes are deposited in NMK, 4 females and 2 males are in TUA. Comments. This species is described based on a good number of females and males obtained from Njuriga (=? Coffea species) in Kenya. It seems to be closely related to T. fuscipennis sp. nov. described above because they share some character states as previously discussed. However, this species is peculiar in this genus in having the pronotum with a median brown marking (Fig. 384), and the drepana on the male abdominal segment IX (Fig, 391).

title: The modal mineralogy of asteroid 162173 Ryugu and its relationship to carbonaceous chondrite meteorites
abstract: &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Introduction: &lt;/strong&gt;Primitive asteroids that accreted beyond the snowline in the protoplanetary disk likely played a crucial role in the delivery of water and organic matter to Earth and other terrestrial planets. The surface of the Cb-type asteroid 162173 Ryugu has low overall reflectance and an absorption feature at ~2.7 &amp;#181;m consistent with the presence of carbonaceous materials and phyllosilicates [1]. The spectral characteristics of Ryugu&amp;#8217;s surface are most similar to the highly altered CI (&amp;#8220;Ivuna-like&amp;#8221;) and/or dehydrated CY (&amp;#8220;Yamato-like&amp;#8221;) carbonaceous chondrites [2].&lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;In December 2020, JAXA&amp;#8217;s Hayabusa2 mission successfully returned to Earth with &gt;5 g of sample collected from the surface of Ryugu. The initial investigation of the samples suggested a close affinity with the CI chondrites [3], which consist of abundant phyllosilicates (~80 vol.%), plus minor amounts of magnetite (~10 vol.%), and dolomite (&lt;5 vol.%), having experienced low temperature (&lt;100&amp;#176;C) aqueous alteration [4]. In contrast, the CY chondrites contain dehydrated phyllosilicates and/or recrystallized olivine (~70 vol.%), Fe-sulphides (up to ~20 vol.%), and sometimes metal (~1 vol.%) following post-hydration metamorphism at temperatures &gt;500&amp;#176;C [5]. Here, as part of the Hayabusa2 &amp;#8220;Stone&amp;#8221; preliminary examination team, we have characterised the modal mineralogy of a Ryugu particle to further constrain its aqueous and thermal history.&lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Methods: &lt;/strong&gt;A powdered sub-sample of Ryugu particle C0002 (plates 3 and 4) was analysed using position-sensitive-detector X-ray diffraction (PSD-XRD) at the Natural History Museum (NHM), London. XRD patterns were acquired from the Ryugu powder using a high-intensity micro X-ray source for 6 hours, with the sample rotated throughout the analysis. Pure standards of each phase detected in the Ryugu powder were analysed under exactly the same conditions for 15 minutes. The modal mineralogy of the Ryugu powder was then determined using an established peak fitting method [4, 5].&lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Results &amp; Discussion:&lt;/strong&gt; Ryugu particle C0002 (plates 3 and 4) contains a mixture of Mg-rich serpentines and smectites that are present at an abundance of ~84 (&amp;#177; 2) vol.%. Other phases identified from the XRD pattern include magnetite (~8 vol.%), pyrrhotite (~7 vol.%), and dolomite (~2 vol.%). This mineralogy is broadly consistent with our petrographic observations of polished Ryugu sections (C0025-01 and C0103-02). Diffraction peaks from anhydrous olivine and pyroxene were not observed suggesting that their abundance is &amp;#8804;1 vol.% in the analysed fraction of C0002. If we assume a maximum anhydrous silicate abundance of 2 vol.%, then the phyllosilicate fraction (PSF = total phyllosilicate abundance / [total anhydrous silicate + total phyllosilicate abundance]) of the Ryugu powder is 0.98, which corresponds to a petrologic sub-type of 1.1 on the alteration scale of Howard et al. [6].&lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The XRD pattern and modal mineralogy of Ryugu particle C0002 (plates 3 and 4) is very similar to the CI chondrites [4]. However, the Ryugu powder does not contain sulphates and ferrihydrite, which are common in the CI chondrites and thought to be terrestrial weathering products [7]. The Ryugu powder also has a comparable mineralogy to the recent C2&lt;sub&gt;ung&lt;/sub&gt; fall Tarda, which appears to be related to the Tagish Lake (C2&lt;sub&gt;ung&lt;/sub&gt;) meteorite [8]. However, Tarda retains partially altered chondrules and has a relatively high abundance of anhydrous silicates (~10 vol.%) [9]. In addition, the XRD pattern and modal mineralogy of the Ryugu powder is clearly distinct from the CY chondrites, which contain dehydrated phyllosilicates that lack coherent diffraction, and abundant poorly crystalline troilite and secondary olivine [5].&lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The modal mineralogy of Ryugu particle C0002 (plates 3 and 4) is consistent with having formed through low temperature aqueous alteration. title: Patania Moore 1888
abstract: Genus Patania Moore, 1888 Patania Moore, 1888: 209. Type species: Botys concatenalis Walker, 1866. Diagnosis. This genus is best distinguished from related genera by (1) the presence of a scale tuft on the male hind tibia (Fig. 2C). In comparison with Pleuroptya, Patania can be further distinguished by the following characters: (2) the wing ground color is dark brownish, with the forewing bearing a pale-yellow comma-shaped spot adjacent to the costa (Fig. 2A) (Pleuroptya: wing ground color usually pale yellow, without such costal maculation; Fig. 2B); (3) in the male genitalia, the median process (‘mp’ in Fig. 4A) of the gnathos is broad and thumb-shaped (Pleuroptya: with or without a slender process; Fig. 4B); (4) the elongate rod-shaped process (‘rp’ in Fig. 4A) extending from the costal base of the valva is distally strongly sclerotized and appears fibula-like (Pleuroptya: narrow distally); (5) the basal sacculus is narrow, with its dorsal margin concave, resulting in a broad transparent membranous area (‘ma’ in Fig. 4A) between the sacculus and fibula (Pleuroptya: basal sacculus broad, dorsal margin straight or slightly convex; transparent membranous area narrow); (6) the hair-pencil sclerite (‘hps’ in Fig. 4A) is large and sac-shaped, bearing specialized scales, including lamellate scales (‘ls’) and comb-like scales (‘cs’) (Pleuroptya: small sclerite only bearing hair-like scales (‘hls’); Fig. 4B). Patania differs from its sister taxon Nosophora in the characters listed above (except for the character 2), and additionally by having a broad, rounded valva (Nosophora: elongate, nearly equal width lengthwise; cf. Matsui et al. 2024a: fig. 5a) and a digitiform fibula (Nosophora: small, plate-like; cf. Matsui et al. 2024a: fig. 5a). Redescription. Male adult (Fig. 2A). Head. Frons smooth. Labial palpus upturned, 2nd palpomere about 7× length of 3rd. Maxillary palpus approximately half length of 2nd labial palpomere. Chaetosemata absent. Antenna ciliate, sensillar setae <1/4 length of flagellomere diameter. Thorax and legs. Metapleuron without scale tuft. Foreleg with tibial epiphysis. Midleg with a pair of tibial spurs, inner spur about 2× length of outer. Hindleg with two pairs of spurs, each inner spur> 5 length of respective outer. Inner side of hind tibial base with a tuft of scales comprising two types: ventral scales flattened, layered, as long as proximal inner spur; dorsal scales short, hair-like (Fig. 2C). Wings. Forewing ground color dark brown; a pale-yellow, comma-shaped spot inward of postmedial line, adjacent to costa; antemedial line dark brown, nearly straight; orbicular stigma dark brown, small, rounded; discoidal stigma dark brown, kidney-shaped; area between orbicular and discoidal stigmata narrowly pale yellow; postmedial line dark brown, incurved from costa to vein M 2, strongly protruding between M 2 and CuA 1, running along with CuA 1 inward, then vertical to dorsum. Hindwing ground color dark brown except basal 2/3 of costal margin; discoidal stigma dark brown, oval; antemedial line not visible; postmedial line indistinct. Cilia concolorous with ground color on both wings. Male retinacular hook absent. Abdomen. Dorsal side concolorous with wings ground color, ventral side whitish. Tympanal organs (Fig 3A, D): fornix tympani broad, strongly protruded ventrally; pons tympani prominent; praecinctorium strongly bifurcate, basally narrow; saccus tympani shallow, posterior margin demarcated by slightly rounded ramus tympani; puteolus tympani narrow, posterior margin demarcated by rounded but medially interrupted venula prima; venula secunda absent. Posterior margin of 2nd sternite thickened as a transverse membranous fold. Male 8th tergite and sternite (Fig. 3G) with broad, subtriangular median sclerotization, anterior margin concave; tergite with a longitudinal stripe on lateral sides posteriorly. Male genitalia (Fig. 4A). Tuba analis long. Subscaphium weakly sclerotized. Uncus nearly trapezoid, distinct from tegumen by intersegmental membrane, apex rounded, dorsally with unsplit setae directed dorsad. Tegumen laterally rounded. Gnathos transverse band-like, with a thumb-shaped median process covered with microsetae (mp in Fig. 4A). Valva broad, costal and apical margins rounded, saccular margin almost straight but protruding ventrad near base; costal base with an elongate rod-shaped process, apically tapering, beyond halfway of costal margin (rp in Fig. 4A); a transparent, membranous area at valval base broad (ma in Fig. 4A); fibula short, finger-like, arising from the membranous area toward distal valva, apex barely sclerotized; sacculus basally narrow, its dorsal margin concave, ventral margin convex. Each transtilla arm with rounded posterior margin, weakly connected medially (separate in Fig. 4A), medio-posterior margin raised as a broad ridge. Juxta shield-shaped, dorsal margin slightly concave. Saccus bulb-shaped, ventral margin without median keel. Phallus cylindrical, with short caecum, ventral apodeme sclerotized as a longitudinal stripe; vesica covered with microspines particularly posterior portion, with a robust, long, sinuate cornutus. Ductus ejaculatorius arising near anterior end of phallus, narrower than phallic diameter, longer than phallus. Hair-pencil sclerite large, sac-shaped, lateral to vinculum; hair-pencils composed of lamellate scales (ls in Fig. 4A), dark-brown comb-like scales (cs in Fig. 4A), dark-brown bending spatulate scales (ss in Fig. 4A), and dark-brown hair-like scales (hls in Fig. 4A). Female genitalia: Not examined. See Kirti & Gill (2007). Species examined. Patania concatenalis. The identification of this species based on the external appearance of the type material preserved in the NHMUK, and the male genitalia illustrated by Kirti & Gill (2007). Remarks. Currently, only the type species can be confidently placed in the strict sense of this genus. Syllepte ningpoalis, the only species added to the Patania subsection by Hampson (1899), may be congeneric; however, the genitalia illustrated by Lee et al. (2021) match those of Nosophora. Patania jatingaensis is the only species described under Patania sensu stricto after Hampson, but the shape and direction of the valva fibula in the male genitalia illustrated in the original description (Rose & Singh 1989) are unusual among Agroterini, suggesting that it is not congeneric. Kirti & Gill (2007) transferred Botys caletoralis Walker, 1859 from Tetridia Warren, 1890 to Patania; however, this treatment was probably based on a misidentification of the species (Mally et al. 2019). Although Kirti & Gill stated that the identity of P. caletoralis had been “confirmed from the Natural History Museum, London,” they did not indicate that they had actually examined the type material, and Mally et al. (2019) were unable to locate the type at NHMUK. Furthermore, the male genitalia of P. caletoralis illustrated by Kirti & Gill differ from those of Patania by the absence of several characters, including the rod-like process from the valval costa, the membranous area at the valval base, and the cornutus. Therefore, we here return Tetridia caletoralis comb. rev. from Patania to Tetridia, pending the re-establishment of the species' identity.

title: Nannopygia ridleyi Kamimura & Cheah & Wang & Lam 2026, comb. nov.
abstract: Nannopygia ridleyi (Kirby, 1903) comb. nov. Figs 1–7 Diplatys ridleyi Kirby, 1903: 61 (Singapore). Literature. Kirby (1903: 61): Singapore (as Diplatys rideleyi) Specimens examined. ZRC • 1 ♀; Bukit Timah Forest; 16 Feb. 1983; D. H. Murphy leg.; Tree bole with termite plastering; ZRC_DER_0000156. • 1 ♂; same data as for ZRC_DER_0000156; ZRC_DER_0000157. Description of male (ZRC _DER_0000156). Length of body (without forceps): 10.4 mm. Length of forceps: 1.8 mm. Head width: 1.4 mm. Pronotum width: 1.0 mm. Pronotum length: 1.1 mm. Color (Figs 2, 3): generally dark brown; mouth parts, antennae (2 nd segment onward), legs pale brown, except dark brownish band on mid femur and base of tibia. Metazona of pronotum, scutellum, and hindwings (except fustis) whitish. Abdomen and forceps reddish brown. Head (Fig. 2): coriaceous with sparse setae, approx. as long as broad, widest in eye region; frons tumid and occiput depressed; transverse suture obsolete, median suture distinct; hind margin widely emarginated in middle; post-ocular carina visible but not prominent, almost straight, running from middle of the internal margin of eyes to the hind margin of the head. Antennae partly broken (only 10 segments remaining in both right and left antenna); first segment stout, expanded apically, length ~ 1 / 2 of the distance between the antennal bases; second segment almost quadrate, small; third segment 1.5 × longer than broad, fourth almost quadrate, shorter than third; fifth segment nearly equal to third, remaining segments gradually lengthening and narrowing distally. Eyes prominent, slightly longer than postocular length. Pronotum (Fig. 2): smooth, approx. as long as broad; anterior and posterior margins widely and gently rounded; sides almost straight, narrowing towards posterior; fore and hind angles rounded; median sulcus distinct; prozona raised and metazona depressed. Tegmina (Fig. 2): well-developed, ~ 2.5 × longer than the pronotum, finely punctulate; humeral angle weak; posterior margins broadly rounded. Hindwings well-developed; length of exposed part almost same as pronotum. Legs long, slender; hind tarsi with first segment ~ 2 × as long as third, second segment ~ 1 / 2 as long as third, claw with arolium. Abdomen (Fig. 2): long, cylindrical, shiny but sparsely punctulate, segments seventh onward gradually expanded. Penultimate sternite (= sternite IX) (Fig. 3): almost quadrate, parallel sided, posterior margin almost truncate with rounded angles and feebly emarginate at middle. Ultimate tergite (Fig. 2): approx. as long as broad, gradually sloping backwards; lateral margins almost straight in anterior 2 / 3 then oblique; hind margin with a pair of swellings at the bases of forceps. Forceps symmetrical, widely separated and strongly curved inward at middle. Genitalia (Figs 4–6): virga with thin, bifurcated tubes, ~ 2 × the length of penis lobe, ellipsoid vesicle at base followed by long common duct, bifurcated part ~ 1 / 5 of entire virgal length, with inner branch conspicuously thicker and longer than outer branch; penis lobe also encloses spindle-shaped sclerite on the outer side; inner side with a smaller rod-shaped sclerite; parameres (Fig. 6) deeply cleft; outer parameral lobe curving inward, acuminate; inner parameral lobe 2 × broader and 1.5 × longer than outer lobe, spatula-shaped but with acute apex pointing inward. Redescription of female (ZRC _DER_0000157) Length of body (without forceps): 8.1 mm. Length of forceps: 1.7 mm. Head width: 1.3 mm. Pronotum width: 1.0 mm. Pronotum length: 1.1 mm. Coloration similar to males but prozona of pronotum paler (Fig. 1). Eyes smaller, approx. as long as postocular length. Forceps (Fig. 1) almost straight, slender, tapering. Distribution. Singapore. Remarks. The external morphology of the adult female specimen from the ZRC closely matches that of the holotype female of Diplatys ridleyi described by Kirby (1903; NHMUK 013323041, Natural History Museum (2025): Fig. 7). Although the paler regions of the holotype appear slightly more yellow, such variation in coloration is common within this group and may reflect the number of days elapsed since emergence and / or preservation environments. Accordingly, we identify both the male and female specimens in the ZRC as belonging to Diplatys ridleyi. Since the original description, based on a holotype collected from an unspecified locality in Singapore, no subsequent records of D. ridleyi have been reported (see Hincks 1955), and the male has remained undescribed. The male specimen described herein exhibits deeply cleft (i. e., bilobed) parameres, a diagnostic feature of the genus Nannopygia Dohrn, 1863 a (= Schizodiplatys Steinmann, 1974). We thus propose Nannopygia ridleyi (Kirby, 1903), comb. nov. Hincks (1957) described Nannopygia malayanus (as Diplatys malayanus) based on a single male specimen collected at Kuala Lumpur, Peninsular Malaysia. He also treated his Diplatys sp. (Hincks 1955) from Mt. Ophir (= Gunung Ledang), Johor State, Peninsular Malaysia, ca 180 km northwest from the center of Singapore Island as a synonym of N. malayanus (Hincks 1957). These two species are very similar, including in the structure of the male genitalia, and are clearly closely related. However, our comparison with the holotype of N. malayanus (NHMUK 013323046: Figs 8–10) reveals the following differences: (1) outer lobes of the parameres wider than the inner lobes in N. malayanus (vs inner lobes wider in the specimen from Singapore); (2) the tips of outer lobes rounded, forming a paddle shape in N. malayanus (vs both inner and outer lobes curve inwardly and acuminate, forming a hook at their apex); (3) inner and outer branches of the bifurcated part of virgae almost same length in N. malayanus (vs longer inner branches); and (4) metazona of pronotum and tarsi much more strongly marked in black in N. malayanus. While this final difference could be attributable to individual variation, the structural differences in (1) to (3) are significant enough to conclude that the two names should not be considered synonyms. Similarly, the external morphology and genitalia of the Singaporean male and female specimens examined in the present study closely resemble those of N. karnyi (Borelli, 1926) known from Indonesia (Mentawai Islands) (Borelli 1926 a; Hincks 1955). However, the male of N. karnyi differs in the following respects: (1) the apex of the outer branch of parameres is thick and almost truncate (vs tapering and distinctly pointed apically in the specimen from Singapore); (2) within each penis lobe, three spine-like (?) structures overlapping the respective virga are present (vs such structures absent); (3) the inner and outer branches of the bifurcated virgae are approximately equal in length (vs the inner branch distinctly longer); and (4) the posterior margin of the penultimate sternite is broadly rounded, with a large oval depression anterior to it (vs nearly truncate with a faint, oval marking). The last character, however, may be attributable to the fact that the specimen from Singapore represents the macrolabic form — within Diplatyidae, intraspecific variation between the macro-, meso-, and microlabic forms has been reported in some species (Hincks 1955; Sakai 1985). The shape of the paramere is also similar to those of N. angustatus (Burr, 1910) from Bangladesh (Burr 1910 b), but this species is characterized by the unique shape of the penultimate sternite with the caudal margin protruding medially, forming a subtruncate lobe (Hincks 1955). Nannopygia appears to have diversified into numerous closely related species in Southeast Asia forming the nigriceps group (Hincks 1955). The present identification is based primarily on the concordance of female external morphology (except for the coloration of the pronotum) among specimens collected from the same locality, rather than on a positive determination derived from detailed examination of male morphology. Further studies on intraspecific variation based on a larger number of specimens, as well as comparative DNA analyses, are desirable.
